groups.label: Code Quality & Guardrails

explore: What would it look like to capture the ctest verification workflow and the v1.0/libc-0.2 branch strategy in a form an agent could read directly?
Which 'never do this' rules (e.g. don't hand-edit generated ctest output, respect the cfg allow-list in build.rs) would be most valuable to make explicit for an assistant?
Is there appetite to try a lightweight AGENTS.md as an experiment before investing in a fuller guide?

roadmap.title: AI involvement in PRs isn't visible or governed yet
roadmap.rationale: With 0% of sampled PRs showing AI involvement and no review bot in the loop, the team has no visibility into whether AI assistance is already happening informally, nor any gate to check AI-suggested changes before they reach the existing human review process.
explore: Is AI assistance already happening informally among contributors, and would surfacing it (e.g. via commit trailers) help the team learn from what's working?
Would an advisory, non-blocking AI review pass on PRs touching cfg/platform logic be worth trying, given how easy it is to introduce a subtle ABI bug there?
What would 'trustworthy enough to merge' look like for an AI-suggested change in a crate this widely depended upon?

roadmap.title: Merges don't currently require an approving review
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection requires 0 approvals and only 38% of merged PRs carry a review today — a thin human safety net that matters more, not less, once AI-assisted contributions start flowing in, since automated suggestions benefit from a verifying second pair of eyes at least as much as human-written code does.
explore: What's the history behind requiring 0 approvals — was it a deliberate call given bors' role in the merge process, or has it just not been revisited?
Would requiring at least one approval on non-trivial PRs change the risk calculus once more AI-assisted contributions start arriving?

roadmap.title: There's no repeatable way to verify AI-proposed changes before they ship
roadmap.rationale: There's no evals/golden-test harness or prompt/agent library, so if AI becomes part of the contribution flow, the only verification available is the existing CI built around human PRs — strong for that purpose, but not framed around checking AI output specifically.
explore: If an agent proposed a new platform binding, would the existing ctest suite alone give the team confidence to merge it, or is something AI-specific missing?
Would sketching a 'definition of done' specifically for AI-assisted PRs help set shared expectations before AI contributions become common?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain verification stops short of code scanning and release signing
roadmap.rationale: Pinned actions and scoped permissions form a solid base, but no SAST scanning and no signed/attested releases mean there's no automated check for either code-level vulnerabilities or release tampering — gaps that matter more as change velocity increases, whether that increase comes from AI assistance or otherwise.
explore: Would a low-noise SAST pass (e.g. CodeQL) surface anything useful in the unsafe FFI surface this crate exposes?
Given how many downstream crates depend on libc, has release signing or provenance ever come up, even informally?

report.headline: A decade-deep, exceptionally rigorous human engineering culture (massive test suite, sophisticated multi-platform CI, mandatory reviewer sign-off) is only beginning to formalize AI-native practice, with real but narrowly-scoped agent guidance and light supply-chain hardening for a project this critical to the world's software supply chain.
strengths: Massive, deeply entrenched automated test suite (49,949 test files, 8.2:1 test/source ratio) validated by one of the most sophisticated multi-platform CI systems in open source
Emerging, concrete AI-agent governance — CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md with real build/test commands and architectural invariants, plus a hard requirement to disclose AI usage in commit messages
A rigorous human review culture via an explicit reviewer-approval workflow visible in every merge commit, even though GitHub's native review-approval metric doesn't capture it
Automated dependency updates and 100% SHA-pinned CI actions reduce supply-chain risk from the tooling side
Long-standing, active contributor cadence sustained over a decade-plus with daily merges
risks: AI agent guidance exists only in one subproject (rust-analyzer) — the vast majority of the compiler/std codebase has no CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, so agents working elsewhere in the tree have no shared conventions to follow
No SAST, no artifact signing/provenance, and no SBOM generation — for a project that compiles a huge fraction of the world's systems software, this is a meaningful supply-chain gap

The detector-reported "0% reviewed PRs" suggests a measurement blind spot (reviewer approval flowing through commit-message tags rather than GitHub's review API) — worth clarifying, since any tool or agent trusting that API would misjudge review rigor
Only 1 required approval and no required status checks/code-owner review encoded in the GitHub-native branch-protection ruleset, which is light for a project of this blast radius
No visible AI code-review/auto-fix bots or LLM-in-CI steps at the main-repo level — agentic workflows remain assistive rather than embedded in the pipeline

Is there a reason the team has stayed with comment/tag-based approval instead of GitHub's built-in review flow?

roadmap.title: Supply-chain hardening stops at dependency freshness and pinning
roadmap.rationale: Dependabot/Renovate and SHA-pinning are in place, but there's no SAST scanning, no artifact signing/provenance, and no SBOM — for a compiler this widely embedded in downstream builds, that's a gap in the kind of verifiable, auditable trail that would let automation (and downstream consumers) trust a release without re-deriving it by hand.
explore: Given how many downstream systems trust rustc binaries, would generating signed provenance or an SBOM for releases change how confidently others can build on them?
Is CodeQL or Semgrep something the team has evaluated for the compiler codebase before, or would it be new ground?

roadmap.title: AI involvement in PRs is effectively invisible in the data
roadmap.rationale: AI-involved PR rate reads 0% and conventional-commit adherence sits at 30% — for a project that already requires AI-usage disclosure in commit messages (per the rust-analyzer CONTRIBUTING reference), there's no visible mechanism surfacing how much AI assistance is actually landing or whether it's reviewed any differently.

roadmap.title: No AI or LLM step rides inside the CI pipeline itself
roadmap.rationale: With four CI workflows already gating build/test, there's room to explore whether an AI review or triage step could sit inside that same gate rather than remaining a purely manual/assistive activity — though for a compiler this size and risk profile, the team may have deliberate reasons for keeping AI out of the merge-gating path.
explore: Has the team considered, or deliberately avoided, an AI-assisted review pass as one more CI signal, given the scale and risk of this codebase?
What would need to be true for an automated suggestion bot to be trusted enough to comment on PRs here?

discrepancies.claim: The signals list "versioned DB migrations" and "progressive delivery / feature flags" for a database-less compiler monorepo — these look like detector false positives (possibly matching Rust's own #![feature(...)] gates or unrelated config) rather than real delivery-as-code practice.

The process signals report 0% reviewed PRs, yet the sampled commit messages show explicit reviewer approval tags on every auto-merge ("r=weihanglo", "r=Mark-Simulacrum", "r=jhpratt", "r=wesleywiser"), indicating the bors/homu merge-queue workflow captures review approval outside GitHub's native review API — the 0% figure is likely a measurement gap, not an absence of review.

"Static type checking (mypy/pyright)" is listed as a signal for a pure-Rust codebase where those Python-specific tools wouldn't normally apply; this looks like a possible false positive or mismatch worth confirming against the triggering file.

CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md were only sampled from src/tools/rust-analyzer/ — if the D1 signal is scoring the whole repo based on this one subdirectory's guidance, it may overstate how broadly agent guidance is applied across the multi-million-line monorepo.

roadmap.rationale: Without something like a CLAUDE.md, every future contributor — human or AI — has to reverse-engineer the workspace layout, the cargo commands, and the gh-pages deploy quirks from scratch, which makes it harder to trust an agent's first attempt at a change here.
explore: What would a new contributor need to know on day one that isn't already spelled out in the README?
Is there a natural place to capture the workspace layout and deploy quirks so an agent doesn't have to guess at them?

roadmap.title: There's no automated test suite behind the availability/manifest logic
roadmap.rationale: Right now the only safety net on a change is manual review, which itself covers just 20% of merged PRs — nothing programmatically confirms that manifest parsing or availability queries still behave correctly, which matters more once any change might be AI-drafted.
explore: Which parts of the manifest/availability logic would be most valuable to lock down with a handful of unit tests first?
Would adding a `cargo test` step to CI change how confident the team feels merging quickly?

roadmap.title: Master can be pushed to directly and the CI workflow carries unscoped tokens
roadmap.rationale: With no branch protection and no explicit `permissions:` block, the deploy job — which already force-pushes to gh-pages — has a more direct path to published output than most teams would want, especially before any agent gets write access to this repo.
explore: What would it take to require at least one review before anything merges to master?
Does the deploy workflow need broader-than-default token permissions, or could it be scoped down to just what it touches?

roadmap.title: CI builds and deploys, but nothing lints, type-checks, or scans dependencies first
roadmap.rationale: The pipeline goes straight from checkout to deploy with no clippy/fmt/test gate and no dependency or SAST scanning, so manual review is currently the only safety net — and that review is only happening on about a fifth of merged PRs.
explore: What would it look like to add a `cargo clippy`/`fmt --check` step before the deploy job runs?
Would a lightweight dependency-update tool be useful here, given the crate pulls in reqwest/serde/chrono?

roadmap.title: AI involvement in the day-to-day workflow is currently invisible in the repo's own signals
roadmap.rationale: None of the sampled commits, PRs, or CI steps show any AI co-authorship or AI review activity — if contributors are already using AI tools informally, none of that shows up yet as a shared, repeatable team capability.
